Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

issues.item: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: These trigger items are not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of mugging/robbery. Physical affection such as hugs is difficult to connect to robbery-related threat activation without any supporting appraisal, memory, or strategy content, and it conflicts with the otherwise stranger/sudden-movement threat profile. Crash imagery is more characteristic of road traffic trauma than robbery and lacks any plausible link to the reported threat items.

issues.item: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: The trigger item about cars being hit in an accident is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of mugging/robbery. The other trigger and threat items coherently suggest interpersonal danger and hypervigilance around strangers/crowding, but crash imagery points to a motor vehicle trauma theme that is not reflected elsewhere in the profile or in the cognitive formulation. This is more than unusual; it appears to reference a different trauma context.

vignette:
Harjinder Singh is a 76-year-old Sikh electrician who has been married for nearly five decades and continues to take on light commercial wiring jobs in the Philadelphia area, a trade he has practiced since immigrating from Punjab in his late twenties. He presented for assessment several months after being robbed at knifepoint outside a hardware supply store on a weekday evening in early autumn. The incident occurred as he was returning to his van after purchasing materials for a job the following morning. A man approached him quickly from the side, smelling strongly of alcohol, and pressed a blade against his ribs while demanding his wallet and phone. Harjinder complied immediately, but the assailant lingered - grabbing his collar, pulling him close enough that the smell of alcohol was overwhelming - before finally running. Harjinder stood alone in the dimly lit parking lot for several minutes afterward, unable to move, his hand pressed flat against the side of his van.

In the weeks that followed, sleep became unreliable and then frightening. He began waking in the early hours from dreams he could not always fully recall, but whose residue - a physical sensation of constriction in his chest, a certainty that something was wrong - stayed with him long after he opened his eyes. On those mornings he would lie still in the dark, listening, unable to shake the feeling that the night around him held something unresolved. He had come to believe, in a way he found difficult to articulate to his wife Paramjit, that darkness itself was no longer neutral. The hours between dusk and dawn felt qualitatively different from daylight - less governed by the ordinary rules that kept people safe - and this conviction had quietly reorganized his evenings. He stopped taking evening jobs, stopped going out after dinner, and began double-checking the locks on the front door before Paramjit had even finished clearing the table.

The work itself, which had always been a source of steady pride, became complicated in new ways. Supply runs that once took twenty minutes now required deliberate mental preparation. Harjinder found that crowded trade counters and busy parking lots produced an immediate, involuntary alertness - a scanning of faces, a positioning of himself near exits. He was certain, in those moments, that proximity to strangers carried a probability of harm that most people around him failed to appreciate. When a fellow contractor reached across him suddenly to grab a circuit breaker from a shelf, Harjinder's body responded before his mind could intervene - a sharp intake of breath, a step backward, hands rising slightly. He was embarrassed by it, and said nothing, but he began timing his supply visits for mid-morning on weekdays, when the stores were quietest, adding an hour of logistical planning to jobs that previously required none.

The smell of alcohol became its own separate difficulty. At a family gathering several weeks after the robbery, a relative poured whisky nearby and the scent reached Harjinder before he had any conscious awareness of the source. What followed was not a thought so much as a physical fact - his body registering threat before his mind caught up. He left the room and did not explain why. He had come to associate that particular smell not with celebration or sociability but with the specific quality of danger he had felt in the parking lot: close, unpredictable, and entirely indifferent to him as a person.

What finally brought Harjinder to seek help was a conversation with Paramjit, who told him quietly one evening that she was worried - not about his safety, but about him. She had noticed that he flinched when their grandson ran toward him in the hallway. He had not noticed it himself until she said it, and the realization unsettled him more than he expected. He is not a man who has sought psychological help before, and he arrived at the intake appointment formal and measured, careful with his words. What he said he most wanted was to stop feeling like a threat was always about to arrive - and to be, once again, the kind of grandfather who could let a child run toward him without his body deciding, before he could, that something was wrong.
